title: Bounded protocols for connected envy-free proportional cake cutting
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: For every fixed integer \(n\ge 4\), does there exist a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) and a finite integer \(B_{n}\) such that, for every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations and all valid query answers, \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) uses at most \(B_{n}\) queries and returns disjoint connected bundles \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{n}\) satisfying \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge \mu _{i}(A_{j})\) for all i,j and \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge 1/n\) for all i, while permitting unallocated cake?
why: Asks whether discarded cake permits exact fairness together with geometric simplicity in finite interaction.

progress.text: Finite exact envy-free protocols are ruled out for complete connected allocation with \(n\ge 3\).
Bounded partial-allocation protocols achieve exact proportionality for three connected recipients, and weaker connected guarantees for larger n.
General bounded protocols give connected partial allocations worth at least \(1/(3n)\) per agent.
A preprint reports single-exponential queries for complete allocation with possibly fragmented bundles.

definitions: The cake is \([0,1]\). Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure \(\mu _{i}\): values are nonnegative and countably additive, \(\mu _{i}([0,1])=1\), and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: \(Eval(i,x,y)\) returns \(\mu _{i}([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a)\), for \(0\le a\le \mu _{i}([x,1])\), returns \(y\ge x\) with \(\mu _{i}([x,y])=a\). Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge \mu _{i}(A_{j})\) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means \(\mu _{i}(A_{i})\ge 1/n\) for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. In this question each \(A_{i}\) must be one interval, up to ownership of its endpoints. The intervals may have gaps between them, and the residue \([0,1]\setminus \bigcup _{i}A_{i}\) may be discarded. Envy is compared with other agents’ assigned intervals, not with the residue. Count every Eval and Cut call as one query. The bound \(B_{n}\) depends only on the fixed n and its protocol, never on the valuation profile or oracle responses. The statement permits a separate finite protocol for each n; it does not require \(B_{n}\) to be polynomial, and does not add an algorithm that generates all \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\).
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a bounded protocol for every fixed \(n\ge 4\), or prove that for at least one fixed \(n\ge 4\) no deterministic protocol and finite bound satisfy the stated guarantees. Existence of a suitable division alone, a procedure that merely converges to one, approximate proportionality, or allowing an agent several intervals does not meet this target.

context_blocks.title: Fairness with one usable piece
context_blocks.text: A connected share is a single interval, as in a continuous appointment slot or one tract of land. Envy-freeness says each person prefers her own assigned interval to anyone else’s. Proportionality additionally protects the amount she receives: at least one n-th of her value for the whole resource.

context_blocks.title: Why disposal changes the question
context_blocks.text: With disposal, giving everyone nothing is envy-free. For example, agents with identical uniform values can each receive an interval of length \(1/(2n)\), leaving half the cake unused; none envies another, but all receive less than their proportional share. The exact \(1/n\) requirement excludes such wasteful outcomes.

context_blocks.title: The connected impossibility has a specific scope
context_blocks.text: Stromquist proves that no finite protocol can always allocate the entire cake envy-freely with one interval per agent once \(n\ge 3\). This assumes complete allocation. Allowing residue is the change studied here, so that theorem does not refute this question.

context_blocks.title: Known partial-allocation guarantees
context_blocks.text: Waste Makes Haste gives a bounded connected envy-free proportional protocol for three agents in its density model. For four agents its connected guarantee is \(1/7\) instead of the required \(1/4\). Aziz and Mackenzie give a bounded connected partial allocation with a \(1/(3n)\) value guarantee in general. These results motivate the question but do not supply exact proportionality for all \(n\ge 4\).

context_blocks.title: Later progress allows fragmented shares
context_blocks.text: The September 2026 Ye–Bai preprint reports a single-exponential query bound for complete envy-free allocation. Complete envy-freeness implies proportionality, but the output may contain multiple intervals per agent. It therefore does not answer this connected-piece question.

sentences: The cake is a divisible interval valued differently by each agent.
The desired division gives every agent one interval, eliminates envy, and guarantees at least one n-th of her value for the whole cake.
Unallocated cake is allowed, but it cannot reduce that proportionality guarantee.
Known connected partial protocols provide weaker guarantees for larger numbers of agents, while recent complete protocols allow fragmented shares.
The question is whether a fixed finite query bound can achieve all the requested properties for every fixed \(n\ge 4\).
